Both PNGs are plain 8-bit RGB without an EXIF orientation tag, so applying the stored orientation (the notebook's load_rgb) leaves the array unchanged; the Rust code decodes the same pixels (checked value by value against the notebook loader). Nothing is resized, cropped or recompressed; only the display copies below are JPEG. Everything is my own Rust code: PNG decoding and hashes, the PCA (src/bin/pca.rs), the 9-tree coding (src/lib.rs), T1 and T2 (src/bin/T1.rs, src/bin/T2.rs) and all figures (drawn with the plotters crate, src/draw.rs). Python is used only for verification: hw7_check.py runs the course notebook's own helpers and compares the PCA model, the decoded T1 pixels and an independent NumPy recount of T2 with the Rust results.

1. Depth

W = 1536, H = 1024. The smallest depth with 3d0 ≥ max(W, H) = 1536 is d0 = 7 (36 = 729 is too small, 37 = 2187 is enough), so the common depth is d = max(7, d0) = 7. At this depth a cell is 1536 / 2187 ≈ 0.702 by 1024 / 2187 ≈ 0.468 pixels: smaller than a pixel, and not a whole pixel.

2. Twelve Codes and Their Pixels

Each prefix is extended with 9 to seven digits. The code is decoded to its continuous rectangle in [0, W) × [0, H) (y downwards, digit layout 1 2 3 / 8 9 4 / 7 6 5), the representative pixel is (⌊xc⌋, ⌊yc⌋) of the rectangle centre. The last column re-encodes the centre of that pixel (x + 0.5, y + 0.5), which is discussed in section 4.

None of these twelve codes share a pixel, because they lie far apart. Sharing does happen for neighbouring deep codes, because a depth-7 cell is narrower than a pixel: 9999999 has centre (768.000, 512.000) and its right neighbour 9999994 has centre (768.702, 512.000); both select pixel (768, 512). Two different addresses, one pixel.

3. Nested Boxes of 1234567

Removing the last digit repeatedly gives 1234567, 123456, …, 1, ROOT. Each box is computed directly from its prefix (integer cell indices, one division), without scanning pixels. The decoded centre of 1234567, (337.4705, 25.0498), stays marked; the parent boxes are not centred on it.

Removing one digit multiplies the width by 3, the height by 3 and the area by 9 (one box is replaced by the parent containing its 3 × 3 siblings). Checks: every decoded centre re-encodes to its own code; every shorter prefix's box contains the previous box and the decoded centre of 1234567. The box widths are exact multiples (ratio 3 within 10−9): the boundaries are computed as (W · index) / 3k, so equal fractions give identical floating-point values at every depth.

4. Region Prefix vs Pixel-Centre Prefix

A code describes a continuous region; a pixel is a 1 × 1 square, and its centre is generally somewhere else. The pixel chosen for 1234567 is (337, 25), whose centre is (337.5, 25.5). The depth-7 cell is y ∈ [24.816, 25.284), and even its depth-4 ancestor 1234 ends at y = 25.284, so the pixel centre lies just below it, in the neighbouring box 1235: the pixel centre encodes to 1235321, which agrees with the region only in the first three digits. In general flooring moves the point by up to one pixel, which is more than one depth-7 cell, so the pixel centre can fall into a neighbouring cell, and if the region is close to a coarse boundary, the codes split early (see the last column above).

5. Resizing or Stretching the Picture

The 9-tree is defined on fractions of the image rectangle, not on pixels. If the same picture is resized or stretched, a prefix still names the same part of the picture (e.g. 1 is always the top-left ninth), but its pixel coordinates change in proportion (x' = x · W'/W, y' = y · H'/H), and a non-uniform stretch changes the shape of every cell. The selected pixel ⌊xc⌋ may change, because rounding depends on the new grid. The depth needed to separate pixel centres depends only on max(W, H): a larger image needs more digits (1920 × 1080 → 7, 3840 × 2160 → 8), a smaller one fewer (≤ 729 pixels → 6).

Task T2: Where are the most frequent colours?

1. PCA Model

One centred, unwhitened PCA on all 1,572,864 pixels of A in RGB/255, computed in Rust: the 3 × 3 covariance matrix of the centred values, its eigenvectors by the Jacobi rotation method, axes sorted by decreasing variance, and each axis signed so that its largest-magnitude loading is positive (the notebook's convention). The result equals the notebook's fit_rgb_pca to within 10−10 (mean, axes including signs, variances). Explained variance: PC1 82.09%, PC2 15.19%, PC3 2.72%. Axis loadings (R, G, B): PC1 = (0.580, 0.562, 0.590) — almost equal weights, i.e. brightness; PC2 = (-0.626, -0.155, 0.764) — blue against red/yellow; PC3 = (-0.521, 0.813, -0.262) — green against red and blue (magenta).

Root rectangles are the full-data min/max of each pair, in original PC units: PC1 ∈ [-0.70420, 1.02749], PC2 ∈ [-0.64568, 0.69341], PC3 ∈ [-0.58249, 0.28879]. No axis has zero range, so no padding was needed. Each axis is divided into thirds of its own range (the rectangles are not forced to be square), depth 4 gives an 81 × 81 grid. The vertical axis follows the plot: the top row (digits 1 2 3) holds the largest vertical values, so the digit diagram looks the same as on the image. Cells are half-open, the root maximum belongs to the last cell.

2. Plots

Scatter plots use a fixed display sample of 30,000 distinct pixels (SplitMix64, seed 2026); the zoomed panels sample up to 30,000 pixels inside the zoom window. All counts use all pixels.

4. Interpretation

Share of the top ten: 4.87% of all pixels in PC1-PC2, 13.40% in PC2-PC3 and 4.39% in PC1-PC3. The colours are spread over thousands of cells; PC2-PC3 concentrates them most, because it drops PC1, the direction with 82% of the variance.

Do the projections agree? Only partly. PC1-PC2 finds very dark, slightly green or brown pixels (shadowed foliage and dark corners): near black, chromatic differences are tiny, so these pixels pile up in a narrow band. PC1-PC3 finds mid-grey cobblestone and wall colours plus the light blue of the sky (ranks 1 and 10). PC2-PC3 also finds neutral greys and the sky blue (rank 7), but its greys range from almost black to light grey, because brightness is not one of its axes. So PC2-PC3 and PC1-PC3 agree on "neutral grey and sky blue", PC1-PC2 points to a different, darker family.

Why projected density can hide differences: a 2D cell only constrains two components; points that differ only in the omitted component fall into the same cell. The clearest case is PC2-PC3 cell 9318: its sampled members include (8, 6, 5) and (138, 129, 134), an almost black and a light grey pixel. They have nearly the same chroma (PC2, PC3) but very different brightness (PC1), which this view does not show. A dense cell therefore means "many pixels share these two coordinates", not "many pixels share one colour".
